newsitem.title: JAPAN: Japan analyst urges easing of LPG stockpile rule.
newsitem.headline: Japan analyst urges easing of LPG stockpile rule.

text.p: Japan's private sector should be allowed to manage its liquefied petroleum gas (LPG) stockpiles more flexibly as a way to stabilise import prices, a private energy think-tank said on Monday.

Toru Mori, an economist with the Institute of Energy Economics (IEE), told reporters that Japanese gas wholesalers should try to stabilise import prices given the recent rise in Saudi Arabia's LPG price.
"One way of doing this is to allow the private sector to manage LPG stockpiles more flexibly when import prices are sharply higher," he said.
Citing rising international LPG prices, Japan relaxed requirements on mandatory LPG stockpiles last December.
Japanese law requires LPG importers to maintain stockpiles equivalent to a minimum of 50 days of imports.
Mori said "further flexible management" would allow importers to maintain a healthy supply-demand balance.
Last December, the government decided to allow importers to temporarily borrow LPG cargoes from other importers to meet required volumes until fresh cargoes arrived.
Saudi Arabia's LPG prices, which have a massive impact on the international LPG market, showed a marked increase last year around the time when the northern hemisphere's winter demand began to grow.
Mori said the Middle East would continue to account for a large share of Japan's LPG imports in 2000, although Saudi Arabia's share could diminish given its own growing demand for liquefied gas.
But the volume supplied by Abu Dhabi could grow, he said.
"The share of LPG supplied by the Middle East will remain large, but the breakdown in the share provided by each country could change," he said.

The Middle East accounted for 78.5 percent of Japan's LPG imports in fiscal 1995/96, according to industry figures, while those from Saudi Arabia were roughly 42 percent and those from Abu Dhabi about 17.3 percent.
